bibl.title: Reconceptualizing synergism and antagonism among multiple stressors

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: TWO WORDS AND THE ARITHMETIC BEHIND THEM - `synergism` and `antagonism` as used for multiple-stressor interactions in ecology, where the same interaction can be both depending on which stressor you take as the reference
span.quote: While the identification of a synergism or antagonism is generally straightforward when both stressors operate in the same direction (i.e., double positive or double negative; Folt et al. 1999 ; Dunne 2010 ), for opposing individual effects, the definition of synergism seems paradoxical because what is synergistic to one stressor's effect direction is antagonistic to the other stressor's effect direction and vice versa. Note that from a purely mathematical perspective, this is not a paradox because synergy can be defined in either direction determined by a larger positive or negative cumulative effect relative to the individual stressor effects in absolute terms.

span.label: how to classify an interaction between two stressors when their individual effects run in opposite directions, and the existing terms give opposite answers depending on the point of view
span.quote: While the identification of a synergism or antagonism is generally straightforward when both stressors operate in the same direction (i.e., double positive or double negative; Folt et al. 1999 ; Dunne 2010 ), for opposing individual effects, the definition of synergism seems paradoxical because what is synergistic to one stressor's effect direction is antagonistic to the other stressor's effect direction and vice versa. Note that from a purely mathematical perspective, this is not a paradox because synergy can be defined in either direction determined by a larger positive or negative cumulative effect relative to the individual stressor effects in absolute terms.

span.label: a directional classification with five classes (+/- synergistic, +/- antagonistic, additive) built on an additive-effects model, a new class called MITIGATING SYNERGISM for reversed-and-enhanced effects, and a reclassification of Crain et al.'s 170-study dataset under it
span.quote: A potentially controversial aspect of the system is the inclusion of a further new class, which we call “mitigating synergism.” In this class, two stressors operating in the same direction create a cumulative effect completely opposite to what would have been predicted; that is, two positives make a negative (−S in “Double positive” row of Table 1 ) or two negatives make a positive (+S in “Double negative” row). Some might argue that such a pattern is the clearest example of antagonism because individual effects are reversed. However, classifying this interaction as antagonistic (according to the currently prevalent definition of this term in the ecological literature) would be misleading in our view because the magnitude of the interaction effect is greater than one would predict based on the two single stressor effects in absolute terms.

span.label: critique
span.quote: As an emerging field in ecology, there are increasing numbers of multiple stressor studies reporting synergisms and antagonisms that are based on imprecise descriptions or simply the judgment of the authors (Dunne 2010 ). These inconsistencies are aggravated by recent reviews and meta-analyses that define and measure these interactions differently and, therefore, are not comparative studies of any exact phenomenon

span.label: a pair of terms in universal use in a field with no committee to standardise them, whose meaning depends on the sign convention of the response variable
span.quote: Despite common use of “synergism” in the scientific literature, a consensus on its operational definition when classifying interactive effects is still lacking (Berenbaum 1989 ; Folt et al. 1999 ; Chou 2010 ; Dunne 2010 ; Vanhoudt et al. 2012 ). In the ecological multiple stressor context, the term most commonly relates to an additive effects model. Thus, synergism is used to define a cumulative effect of multiple stressors that are greater than the additive sum of effects produced by the stressors acting in isolation; this contrasts with the term “antagonism,” used to define a cumulative effect that is less than additive

span.label: conceptual analysis plus reclassification: the directional scheme is applied to the 170-study dataset compiled by Crain et al. (2008) and the resulting class frequencies compared against the original analysis of the same data
span.term: conceptual analysis plus reclassification: the directional scheme is applied to the 170-study dataset compiled by Crain et al. (2008) and the resulting class frequencies compared against the original analysis of the same data
span.quote: Together with our reclassification of four double-positive antagonisms as negative synergisms, this accounts for the discrepancy in the (direction-independent) prevalence of interaction classes between our overall findings of 43% antagonism, 31% synergism, and 26% additive, versus Crain et al. ( 2008 ) 38% antagonism, 36% synergism, and 26% additive based on an identical dataset.

span.label: **THE SAME 170 STUDIES, TWO DEFINITIONS, DIFFERENT ANSWERS**: `this accounts for the discrepancy in the (direction-independent) prevalence of interaction classes between our overall findings of 43% ANTAGONISM, 31% SYNERGISM, AND 26% ADDITIVE, versus Crain et al. (2008) 38% ANTAGONISM, 36% SYNERGISM, AND 26% ADDITIVE **BASED ON AN IDENTICAL DATASET**.` Not two cohorts, not two instruments, not two decades - THE SAME DATA RECLASSIFIED. The cleanest demonstration in this corpus that a definition changes the number
span.quote: Together with our reclassification of four double-positive antagonisms as negative synergisms, this accounts for the discrepancy in the (direction-independent) prevalence of interaction classes between our overall findings of 43% antagonism, 31% synergism, and 26% additive, versus Crain et al. ( 2008 ) 38% antagonism, 36% synergism, and 26% additive based on an identical dataset.

span.label: AND THE RECLASSIFICATION IS ITEMISED: `Of the 49 OPPOSING interactions classified by Crain et al., we RECLASSIFIED THREE ANTAGONISMS AS POSITIVE SYNERGISMS ... and ELEVEN SYNERGISMS AS POSITIVE ANTAGONISMS ... Thus, Crain et al.'s conceptualization of synergism and antagonism for interactions involving stressors with opposing individual effects UNDERREPRESENTED POSITIVE SYNERGISMS (BECAUSE THEY WERE NOT POSSIBLE) but OVERREPRESENTED NEGATIVE SYNERGISMS.` A class that could not be counted because the definition had no name for it
span.quote: Of the 49 opposing interactions classified by Crain et al. ( 2008 ), we reclassified three antagonisms as positive synergisms (enhanced positive effect when negative stressor present) and eleven synergisms as positive antagonisms (less positive than predicted additively, but less negative than the negative stressor alone). Thus, Crain et al.'s ( 2008 ) conceptualization of synergism and antagonism for interactions involving stressors with opposing individual effects underrepresented positive synergisms (because they were not possible) but overrepresented negative synergisms.

span.label: **AND THE TERM IS PARADOXICAL BY CONSTRUCTION**: `for opposing individual effects, THE DEFINITION OF SYNERGISM SEEMS PARADOXICAL BECAUSE WHAT IS SYNERGISTIC TO ONE STRESSOR'S EFFECT DIRECTION IS ANTAGONISTIC TO THE OTHER STRESSOR'S EFFECT DIRECTION AND VICE VERSA.` The same interaction carries both labels at once, and which one you report is a choice of reference point rather than a finding
span.quote: While the identification of a synergism or antagonism is generally straightforward when both stressors operate in the same direction (i.e., double positive or double negative; Folt et al. 1999 ; Dunne 2010 ), for opposing individual effects, the definition of synergism seems paradoxical because what is synergistic to one stressor's effect direction is antagonistic to the other stressor's effect direction and vice versa. Note that from a purely mathematical perspective, this is not a paradox because synergy can be defined in either direction determined by a larger positive or negative cumulative effect relative to the individual stressor effects in absolute terms.

span.label: AND THE VERDICT FLIPS WITH THE SIGN CONVENTION OF THE RESPONSE VARIABLE: `This interactive pattern of leaf decay could be presented either POSITIVELY (as RATE OF LEAF MASS LOSS) or NEGATIVELY (as LEAF MASS REMAINING). DEPENDING ON WHICH PERSPECTIVE WAS ASSUMED IN THE ANALYSIS, ONE COULD CONCLUDE SYNERGISM FOR LEAF MASS REMAINING OR ANTAGONISM FOR RATE OF LOSS, yet the interaction is CLEARLY SYNERGISTIC.` One measurement, two ways of writing it down, two opposite classifications - and no experiment can settle it
span.quote: Take the example of a data set for decomposition of leaf matter where nutrient enrichment alone accelerates decay while sediment addition alone slows decay, but both stressors in combination cause a decay rate even greater than with nutrient enrichment alone. This interactive pattern of leaf decay could be presented either positively (as rate of leaf mass loss) or negatively (as leaf mass remaining). Depending on which perspective was assumed in the analysis, one could conclude synergism for leaf mass remaining or antagonism for rate of loss, yet the interaction is clearly synergistic

span.label: **AND TWO META-ANALYSES DISAGREE BY SEVENTEEN POINTS FOR THE SAME REASON**: `Holmstrup et al. (2010) reported synergisms in OVER HALF of their studies, whereas Darling and Cote (2008) reported synergisms in ONLY A THIRD, MOST LIKELY REFLECTING THE UPWARD BIAS OF HOLMSTRUP ET AL.'S DEFINITION OF SYNERGY VERSUS DARLING AND COTE'S DOWNWARD BIAS.` And the general form: `recent reviews and meta-analyses that DEFINE AND MEASURE THESE INTERACTIONS DIFFERENTLY and, therefore, ARE NOT COMPARATIVE STUDIES OF ANY EXACT PHENOMENON`
span.quote: Not surprisingly, Holmstrup et al. ( 2010 ) reported synergisms in over half of their studies, whereas Darling and Cote ( 2008 ) reported synergisms in only a third, most likely reflecting the upward bias of Holmstrup et al.'s ( 2010 ) definition of synergy versus Darling and Cote's ( 2008 ) downward bias (a weakness of an additive effects model when individual effects are large or numerous; Folt et al. 1999 ).

span.label: AND THE SAME PHENOMENON HAS ANOTHER FIELD'S NAME: `IN TOXICOLOGY, IN CONTRAST TO ECOLOGICAL USAGE, if one chemical is rendered more effective by the presence of another that has no effect or a different effect on its own, THE INTERACTION IS CALLED POTENTIATION OR SENSITIZATION. Chou (2010) argues that this interaction type IS NOT A TRUE SYNERGISM because it is `ONE-SIDED` and the underlying MODES OF ACTION ARE DIFFERENT.` A cross-field renaming AND a dispute about whether the case falls under the term at all, in two sentences
span.quote: In toxicology, in contrast to ecological usage, if one chemical is rendered more effective by the presence of another that has no effect or a different effect on its own, the interaction is called potentiation or sensitization (Odum and Barrett 2005 ). Chou ( 2010 ) argues that this interaction type is not a true synergism because it is “one-sided” and the underlying modes of action are different. If this perspective was to be generally accepted, the term synergy would only apply when both stressors operate in the same direction.

span.label: AND A THIRD FIELD HAS A THIRD NAME FOR THE NEW CLASS: `In EPIDEMIOLOGICAL RESEARCH, such SO-CALLED CROSSOVER INTERACTIONS are considered THE MOST STATISTICALLY ROBUST CLASS OF INTERACTION because they indicate that risk factors FLIP FROM BEING DISEASE PREDISPOSING IN ONE BACKGROUND TO PROTECTIVE IN ANOTHER. There is, however, DEEP CONTROVERSY surrounding the expected prevalence of such interactions between epidemiologists.` Ecology's `mitigating synergism` is epidemiology's `crossover interaction`, and the two fields disagree about how often it happens
span.quote: Moreover, such strong interactions may have the most interesting ecological consequences because they suggest that when both stressors act together, they synergistically mitigate or inhibit their individual effects even more than under control conditions (i.e., effect reversal with enhancement). In epidemiological research, such so-called crossover interactions are considered the most statistically robust class of interaction because they indicate that risk factors flip from being disease predisposing in one background to protective in another (Kendler and Gardner 2010 ). There is, however, deep controversy surrounding the expected prevalence of such interactions between epidemiologists

span.label: AND THE PHENOMENON WAS OBSERVED BEFORE IT WAS NAMED: `A recent review ... by Strain et al. (2014) utilized a directional interaction classification that DOCUMENTED EXAMPLES OF MITIGATING SYNERGISMS, ALTHOUGH THEY DID NOT USE THE TERM. However, their approach NEGLECTED TO DISTINGUISH ANTAGONISM IN SITUATIONS WHERE STRESSOR EFFECTS WERE OPPOSING.` The instances were in the literature with nothing to call them - which is what a missing term looks like from outside
span.quote: A recent review of the interacting roles of stressors driving the global loss of canopy-forming to mat-forming algae in marine ecosystems by Strain et al. ( 2014 ) utilized a directional interaction classification that documented examples of mitigating synergisms, although they did not use the term. However, their approach neglected to distinguish antagonism in situations where stressor effects were opposing.

span.label: AND A TERM IS REDEFINED TO REMOVE AN ASSUMPTION BURIED IN IT: `the term `STRESSOR` has frequently been used SYNONYMOUSLY WITH `POLLUTION,` `POLLUTANTS,` OR `PRESSURES` ON THE ASSUMPTION THAT THE EFFECTS OF A STRESSOR IMPLY `STRESS` AND MUST THEREFORE BE EXCLUSIVELY DETRIMENTAL. However, WHAT IS STRESSFUL OR DETRIMENTAL TO ONE SPECIES IN AN ECOSYSTEM IS LIKELY TO BE BENEFICIAL TO ANOTHER ... Therefore, WE DEFINE A STRESSOR AS A VARIABLE THAT ... AFFECTS (WHETHER NEGATIVELY OR POSITIVELY)`. The word carried a sign, and the redefinition removes it
span.quote: In ecological research, the term “stressor” has frequently been used synonymously with “pollution,” “pollutants,” or “pressures” on the assumption that the effects of a stressor imply “stress” and must therefore be exclusively detrimental (Folt et al. 1999 ). However, what is stressful or detrimental to one species in an ecosystem is likely to be beneficial to another, either directly or via species interactions. Moreover, stressor responses may follow a subsidy-stress gradient, as observed, for example, for stream taxa in relation to dissolved nutrient concentration (Niyogi et al. 2007 ). Therefore, we define a stressor as a variable that, as a result of human activity, exceeds its range of normal variation and affects (whether negatively or positively) individual taxa, community composition, or ecosystem functioning relative to a reference condition

span.label: AND ANOTHER GROUP SOLVED THE SAME PROBLEM BY INVENTING ITS OWN VOCABULARY: `Vanhoudt et al. (2012) applied THEIR OWN DEFINITIONS of synergism and antagonism based on `Concentration Addition` or `Independent Action` toxicological models. Due to the LACK OF SUPPORT FOR EITHER OF THESE MODELS, the authors then DEVISED THEIR OWN SIMPLIFYING TERMINOLOGY to give an overview of their results as `POSITIVE INTERACTIONS` (describing additive, synergism, `superaddition,` `potentiation,` or `increased effects`), `NEGATIVE INTERACTIONS` (loosely, antagonism), or no interactions.` Five terms collapsed into one, because none of them could be measured
span.quote: Acknowledging these differences of interpretation, Vanhoudt et al. ( 2012 ) applied their own definitions of synergism and antagonism based on “Concentration Addition” or “Independent Action” toxicological models. Due to the lack of support for either of these models, the authors then devised their own simplifying terminology to give an overview of their results as “positive interactions” (describing additive, synergism, “superaddition,” “potentiation,” or “increased effects”), “negative interactions” (loosely, antagonism), or no interactions.

span.label: THE FIELD REPORTS THESE TERMS WITHOUT DEFINING THEM: `there are increasing numbers of multiple stressor studies reporting synergisms and antagonisms that are BASED ON IMPRECISE DESCRIPTIONS OR SIMPLY THE JUDGMENT OF THE AUTHORS. These inconsistencies are aggravated by recent reviews and meta-analyses that DEFINE AND MEASURE THESE INTERACTIONS DIFFERENTLY and, therefore, ARE NOT COMPARATIVE STUDIES OF ANY EXACT PHENOMENON.` The strongest sentence in this corpus about what a shared word without a shared definition does to a literature
span.quote: As an emerging field in ecology, there are increasing numbers of multiple stressor studies reporting synergisms and antagonisms that are based on imprecise descriptions or simply the judgment of the authors (Dunne 2010 ). These inconsistencies are aggravated by recent reviews and meta-analyses that define and measure these interactions differently and, therefore, are not comparative studies of any exact phenomenon

span.label: AND THE FIELD IS BIASED IN THE DIRECTION IT LOOKS: `This is particularly pertinent given THE BIAS TOWARD INVESTIGATING AND REPORTING ADVERSE MULTIPLE STRESSOR EFFECTS (i.e., DOUBLE-NEGATIVE INTERACTION TYPE) IN ECOLOGY.` The class frequencies are conditioned on which interactions anybody bothered to study, and the paper says so in the sentence that reports them
span.quote: Our finding that the representation of interaction classes varied markedly by interaction type highlights the need to consider the direction of individual stressor effects when determining the occurrence of synergisms and antagonisms. This is particularly pertinent given the bias toward investigating and reporting adverse multiple stressor effects (i.e., double-negative interaction type) in ecology

span.label: AND THE NEW CLASS IS CONCEDED TO BE ARGUABLE: `SOME MIGHT ARGUE THAT SUCH A PATTERN IS THE CLEAREST EXAMPLE OF ANTAGONISM because individual effects are reversed. However, classifying this interaction as antagonistic (according to the currently prevalent definition of this term in the ecological literature) WOULD BE MISLEADING IN OUR VIEW.` The objection is stated in the paper's own words before anyone else can make it
span.quote: A potentially controversial aspect of the system is the inclusion of a further new class, which we call “mitigating synergism.” In this class, two stressors operating in the same direction create a cumulative effect completely opposite to what would have been predicted; that is, two positives make a negative (−S in “Double positive” row of Table 1 ) or two negatives make a positive (+S in “Double negative” row). Some might argue that such a pattern is the clearest example of antagonism because individual effects are reversed. However, classifying this interaction as antagonistic (according to the currently prevalent definition of this term in the ecological literature) would be misleading in our view because the magnitude of the interaction effect is greater than one would predict based on the two single stressor effects in absolute terms.

span.label: and a method imported from another field carries that field's assumptions: `isobolographic analysis ... seems of LIMITED UTILITY IN MANY ECOLOGICAL CONTEXTS because it relies on establishing multiple levels of dose-concentration relationships ... and is further limited by IMPLICITLY ASSUMING SYNERGY ONLY WHEN EFFECTS ARE NEGATIVE, REFLECTING ITS TOXICOLOGICAL ORIGINS.` The instrument's home discipline is inside the instrument
span.quote: Alternative approaches for inferring synergism and antagonism utilizing isobolographic analysis exist in the fields of pharmacology, toxicology, and pathology (Nelson and Kursar 1999 ). While isobolographic analysis presents some key advantages over additive and multiplicative models (see Dunne 2010 ), it seems of limited utility in many ecological contexts because it relies on establishing multiple levels of dose–concentration relationships (a substantial ecological challenge in itself) and is further limited by implicitly assuming synergy only when effects are negative, reflecting its toxicological origins.

span.label: applying the new directional classification to the SAME dataset Crain et al. (2008) used, rather than to a new one
span.note: eliminates: a difference in prevalence caused by different studies rather than by different definitions · outcome: held
span.quote: Together with our reclassification of four double-positive antagonisms as negative synergisms, this accounts for the discrepancy in the (direction-independent) prevalence of interaction classes between our overall findings of 43% antagonism, 31% synergism, and 26% additive, versus Crain et al. ( 2008 ) 38% antagonism, 36% synergism, and 26% additive based on an identical dataset.

span.label: an additive effects model as the null, chosen for consistency with the prevailing definition of synergy and with ANOVA
span.note: eliminates: a classification whose null model differs from the one the field's statistics already assume · outcome: partial
span.quote: The approach is potentially adaptable for testing against a multiplicative model (i.e., log additive; Folt et al. 1999 ). However, in this case, we recommend following the advice of Folt et al. ( 1999 ) that nonadditive responses should not be called synergisms or antagonisms so as to avoid confusion with the additive model.

span.label: reporting the directional class (+S, -S, +A, -A) alongside the direction-independent one
span.note: eliminates: the loss of information that makes a positive synergism unnameable and therefore uncountable · outcome: held
span.quote: Of the 49 opposing interactions classified by Crain et al. ( 2008 ), we reclassified three antagonisms as positive synergisms (enhanced positive effect when negative stressor present) and eleven synergisms as positive antagonisms (less positive than predicted additively, but less negative than the negative stressor alone). Thus, Crain et al.'s ( 2008 ) conceptualization of synergism and antagonism for interactions involving stressors with opposing individual effects underrepresented positive synergisms (because they were not possible) but overrepresented negative synergisms.

span.quote: While the identification of a synergism or antagonism is generally straightforward when both stressors operate in the same direction (i.e., double positive or double negative; Folt et al. 1999 ; Dunne 2010 ), for opposing individual effects, the definition of synergism seems paradoxical because what is synergistic to one stressor's effect direction is antagonistic to the other stressor's effect direction and vice versa. Note that from a purely mathematical perspective, this is not a paradox because synergy can be defined in either direction determined by a larger positive or negative cumulative effect relative to the individual stressor effects in absolute terms.

span.quote: In toxicology, in contrast to ecological usage, if one chemical is rendered more effective by the presence of another that has no effect or a different effect on its own, the interaction is called potentiation or sensitization (Odum and Barrett 2005 ). Chou ( 2010 ) argues that this interaction type is not a true synergism because it is “one-sided” and the underlying modes of action are different. If this perspective was to be generally accepted, the term synergy would only apply when both stressors operate in the same direction.

However, classifying this interaction as antagonistic (according to the currently prevalent definition of this term in the ecological literature) would be misleading in our view because the magnitude of the interaction effect is greater than one would predict based on the two single stressor effects in absolute terms.

span.quote: In ecological research, the term “stressor” has frequently been used synonymously with “pollution,” “pollutants,” or “pressures” on the assumption that the effects of a stressor imply “stress” and must therefore be exclusively detrimental (Folt et al. 1999 ). However, what is stressful or detrimental to one species in an ecosystem is likely to be beneficial to another, either directly or via species interactions. Moreover, stressor responses may follow a subsidy-stress gradient, as observed, for example, for stream taxa in relation to dissolved nutrient concentration (Niyogi et al. 2007 ). Therefore, we define a stressor as a variable that, as a result of human activity, exceeds its range of normal variation and affects (whether negatively or positively) individual taxa, community composition, or ecosystem functioning relative to a reference condition

Thus, synergism is used to define a cumulative effect of multiple stressors that are greater than the additive sum of effects produced by the stressors acting in isolation; this contrasts with the term “antagonism,” used to define a cumulative effect that is less than additive

span.quote: Despite common use of “synergism” in the scientific literature, a consensus on its operational definition when classifying interactive effects is still lacking (Berenbaum 1989 ; Folt et al. 1999 ; Chou 2010 ; Dunne 2010 ; Vanhoudt et al. 2012 ). In the ecological multiple stressor context, the term most commonly relates to an additive effects model. Thus, synergism is used to define a cumulative effect of multiple stressors that are greater than the additive sum of effects produced by the stressors acting in isolation; this contrasts with the term “antagonism,” used to define a cumulative effect that is less than additive

span.quote: In ecological research, the term “stressor” has frequently been used synonymously with “pollution,” “pollutants,” or “pressures” on the assumption that the effects of a stressor imply “stress” and must therefore be exclusively detrimental (Folt et al. 1999 ). However, what is stressful or detrimental to one species in an ecosystem is likely to be beneficial to another, either directly or via species interactions. Moreover, stressor responses may follow a subsidy-stress gradient, as observed, for example, for stream taxa in relation to dissolved nutrient concentration (Niyogi et al. 2007 ). Therefore, we define a stressor as a variable that, as a result of human activity, exceeds its range of normal variation and affects (whether negatively or positively) individual taxa, community composition, or ecosystem functioning relative to a reference condition
